title: Nostradamus: Predictor of the future? Not so much.
summary: Josh and Chuck examine Nostradamus, separating the biography from the myth: his birth name and Latinized name, his astrology and medical career, plague work, the Centuries quatrains and their vague, translation-prone wording, the Hitler "Hstor" quatrain, the Henry II prophecy, and the 9/11 quatrain hoax (Neil Marshall's demonstration). They close with the ClickHole Adam Sandler satire and a listener mail about Oregon Trailer camp trailers.

segments.title: Opening banter and Nostradamus introduction
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about Nostradamus-style vague predictions and reminisce about past interest in occult topics, then set out to separate the man from the myth.

segments.title: Early life, name, and astrology
segments.summary: Nostradamus was born Michel de Nostredame in France, Latinized his name after medical school, and had a family that valued education and possibly converso background. He practiced astrology, making more specific predictions than his peers, which earned their disdain.

segments.title: Medical career, plague, and wandering years
segments.summary: He became a physician who treated plague victims and promoted sanitation, fresh air and a rose hip lozenge. After his wife and children died, he left his village after a joke about a Virgin Mary statue drew the Inquisition, and he traveled Europe, remarrying before settling in Salon.

segments.title: The Centuries and its success
segments.summary: In Salon he published his book of prophecies, originally called the Prophecies and later known as The Centuries, consisting of about a thousand quatrains. Printing presses, the dark times of religious war, and a superstitious queen helped make it a sensation, and Catherine de Medici invited him to court.

segments.title: Trance method, obscure wording, and translation problems
segments.summary: Nostradamus reportedly gazed into flames or bowls of herbs, possibly ingesting nutmeg, and claimed angelic help. He reportedly wrote obscurely to avoid persecution. Hosts discuss how early printing errors and translation variations, plus the Villeneuve example, allow many interpretations.

segments.title: Hitler quatrain, Henry II prophecy, and skeptical arguments
segments.summary: The 'Histor' quatrain is read as Hitler by believers, though Histor is the lower Danube; the Nazis used it in pamphlets. The Henry II death quatrain is discussed as coming true through a jousting accident. Skeptics argue statistically that vague predictions will eventually match events and that predictions are only identified after the fact.

segments.title: 9/11 quatrain hoax and other misattributed predictions
segments.summary: After 9/11 a quatrain was circulated as a prediction of the attacks, but it was written by Neil Marshall, a Canadian student, as a demonstration of how gullible readers are. Other quatrains were combined to support claims about Mabus and Usama bin Laden, and a 1999 end-of-the-world date was recalculated. The Coup's album cover was changed after 9/11.

segments.title: ClickHole Adam Sandler satire and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the viral ClickHole satire claiming Adam Sandler predicted tragedies, then listener mail about Oregon Trailer camp trailers and contact information, and the closing.
